title: “Floating Scarecrow” Demonstrates the Enduring Power of Eyes in the Natural World - Nautilus
gist: A new study suggests eye-pattern 'floating scarecrows' could reduce seabird bycatch in European gillnets, where 95,000 diving seabirds are entangled each year — echoing a 1980s Indian Forestry Service trick of rear-facing face masks that deterred Bengal tiger attacks.

insights.claim: In the 1980s the Indian Forestry Service handed out thousands of cheap rubber masks worn on the back of the head to deter Bengal tigers that attacked fishermen, honey collectors and wood cutters from behind, and the trick worked at least for a while.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Cheap behavioral deterrents can solve costly wildlife-conflict problems — a low-capex template for mitigation tech.
insights.quote: Remarkably, the subterfuge worked (at least for a while).
insights.locator: In the 1980s, the Indian Forestry Service

insights.claim: The tiger-mask idea was inspired by artificial eyespots that insects evolved to ward off predators, on the logic that predators that attack only from behind would be deterred by a pair of watching eyes.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Biomimetic, low-cost design principle with potential applications beyond wildlife.
insights.locator: In the 1980s, the Indian Forestry Service

insights.claim: Every year about 95,000 diving seabirds get caught in gillnets off the coast of Europe, chiefly auks such as guillemots and razorbills that are drawn to fish snagged in the vertical nets and drown.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Quantifies a bycatch problem that drives fisheries regulation and potential gear-mandate costs for European fishing fleets.
insights.quote: Every year, 95,000 diving seabirds get caught in gillnets off the coast of Europe.

insights.claim: Seabird bycatch in European gillnets worsens in winter months because fisheries reduce the size of their net holes.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Seasonal gear choices drive bycatch peaks, so mitigation rules would likely target winter fisheries.

insights.claim: A new study suggests the eye-pattern deterrence principle — a 'floating scarecrow' — could help keep seabirds from entangling themselves in fishing nets.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Cheap passive deterrents could offer fisheries a low-cost compliance path versus closures or gear bans.
insights.locator: In the 1980s, the Indian Forestry Service
